title: What to Expect From the Music of ‘MST3K: The RiffTrax Experiments,’ According to Mike, Kevin & Bill
summary: As they return to the Satellite of Love, Michael J. Nelson, Kevin Murphy and Bill Corbett delve into the show's song parody history and what's yet to come.
contentText:
Mystery Science Theater 3000 — a show about a human and bric-a-brac robot puppets who watch cinematic dreck while slinging high and lowbrow quips — is perhaps TV’s longest, strangest trip.

Like a beloved B-movie monster, the show refuses to die. Since 1988, MST3K has found on-and-off life via public access television, cable TV, streaming services and fan-funded episodes, all thanks to a loyal cult audience that celebrates its willfully obscure, proudly niche comedy. ( MST3K is now owned by Radial Entertainment, which purchased it from creator Joel Hodgson earlier this year.)

So strong is the ongoing hunger for the show’s offbeat humor that when RiffTrax — a 20-year-old movie-mocking franchise featuring MST3K alumni Michael J. Nelson, Kevin Murphy and Bill Corbett — announced a crossover MST3K comeback, the Kickstarter for Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments exploded.

In February, Nelson (who hosted the show from 1993-1999), Murphy (Tom Servo from 1990-1999) and Corbett (Crow from 1997-1999, 2020) asked for $20,000 to fund a four-episode return to the Satellite of Love using practical effects; a month later, they got $2.7 million. (That’s some serious sampo .)

Ahead of the first episode hitting movie theaters on Sept. 9 and Sept. 13 (via Fathom Entertainment and RiffTrax) and backers’ accounts in October, Billboard spoke to Nelson, Murphy and Corbett about the show’s musical history and what the tuneful troika is bringing to these four new episodes. We delve into song scribe Nelson’s creative process back in the day (his Minnesota digs were slightly less spacious than Prince’s Paisley Park complex six miles away); what to expect from Jonathan Coulton ’s new version of the theme song; fresh music moments in the upcoming experiments; and beating South Park to the Canada-roasting punch by one year with their “eh”-plus anthem back in the ’90s.

Congrats on blowing past that Kickstarter goal. That must have been insanely gratifying.

Kevin Murphy : It was a big vote of confidence for what we’re doing, and it was very encouraging. It inspired us to have as much fun with this as we could.

Mike, you’ve written a lot of songs for the show’s host segments. How does that happen? Does someone say, “A song would be nice in this sketch?” Are you like, “oh, I have this girl group parody that makes sense for a werewolf episode”?

Michael J. Nelson : When I was doing the music, my keyboard and I were in a closet. It was the phone closet — the phone, not foam closet — where the switching would happen for the phones. It was just like, “Hey, that’s big enough for you.” So my keyboard was in a closet on the side of the stage, and people would just go, “Hey, we need a song.” And look, I’m not Neil Diamond, guys.

Bill Corbett: Come on. You’re forever in blue jeans.

Nelson : I would sit at a keyboard, and people would be like, “Hey, we need a song about this.” I’d be in the writing room, but I would go into this closet, and people would open the closet door and go, “How’s it going with that song?”

Corbett : And you would be in there, nude.

Mike : Why were my pants constantly off? I don’t know. Weird. No, it was just funny. It wasn’t like this, but it felt like someone would yell in, “Hey, song boy!” But anyway, that’s where I wrote it. It was a 3 x 3 closet.

How much time does it take you playing around on a keyboard to come up with something?

Nelson : Well, it’s like the old cliché: “What is your motivation?” Like, my paycheck. I have to do that today; I have to get this done. We’re gonna do the read-through at three or whatever, so it has to be done by now. So I have to present this song to the people, and then they would all crowd around my little closet, and I would play the little song. And literally that happened many, many times.

Murphy : Oh, yeah.

And thunderous applause after that?

Nelson : Dead silence, mostly. But I don’t care. It’s like, “Look, we got to put it up tomorrow. What are you going to do? You’re going to write a different song?”

How do you decide who writes the lyrics? Bill, when you wrote the lyrics for “ The Canada Song ,” was it like, “I’ve got some grievances about Canada to get off my chest”?

Corbett : Well, when we would do the ideas for sketches on our classic whiteboard — actually, we had a corkboard then, with index cards — some of them were just like, “maybe we should do a thing where we unreasonably — unreasonably — hate Canada, and then Servo comes on to defend it.” So that could have been a sketch, but it just felt like it would be funnier as a song. I don’t even remember enough to know how we decided that. But I knew that if I wrote something that was kind of anthemic like that, then I’d say, “Mike, this needs to be kind of like an anthem, kind of jaunty.”

Murphy : [Starts humming jaunty tune.]

Corbett : He’s just a master of going between genres. And luckily, it didn’t need to be Sondheim-sophisticated in terms of music — although Mike often delivered that too, and so did Kevin. That’s the process as I remember it. We have a funny idea first, and then maybe sometimes there’s something in the movie that just says “song” right away to somebody, and they come in: I really want to write a song about Patrick Swayze at Christmas. But mostly comedy first, and then, “Hey, we haven’t done a song in a while. Let’s try that. Do we have the time? Do we have the resources? Would it make a good song?” But I’m glad we did it. It’s some of my favorite stuff to sing and write and watch.

So many of them are fan favorites. I don’t know how much you can tease, but can we expect some host musical moments in these upcoming episodes?

Murphy : Oh yeah, definitely.

How did you approach those? Was there pressure to deliver?

Corbett : There’s really no pressure, because it’s all us. I think we have an instinct for mixing it up a little. If we have some wordy sketches or some prop-heavy sketches, maybe we do a song for the next one — and maybe we combine prop-heavy and song, which is one of the songs we did. It’s just an instinct to entertain and be amusing. Vaudeville, my young friend!

Murphy : I was going to say, it’s sort of Tin Pan Alley. But the movie inspires the song quite often. Watching the movie, we used to do it writing-room style, and suddenly you’d see this scene and you’d say, “I feel a song coming on.” I mean, just that corny. And you say, “What they’re talking about right now would be the subject for a great song.”

I did want to ask you specifically, Kevin — first off, you have a great voice.

Murphy : Thank you.

Corbett : Like an angel! Like a freakin’ angel!

A lot of the moments when Servo starts singing feel organic, like the spirit of song seized you. Is that really what it was like in the writers’ room? You’re watching and you start singing along?

Murphy : Sometimes, I can’t recall how many times, there’s some corny little ditty going on in the movie, and we just start singing to it, because the ditty is caught in your ear, and you just reflexively start singing to it.

Nelson : I will say, a little preview here: there’s at least one movie in our four [episodes] where that is very much the impetus for the song. I’ll add one thing. Once — this is back in the ’90s — we went to the movie studios and we’re like, “Hey, all these puppets, how about we sing a lot?” And they’re like, “We do not like singing or songs at all. We just tested a movie — we hate music.” And it’s like, “Oh, we kind of thought that the script would be filled with songs.”

Murphy : Yep. Our pitch was all singing, all dancing.

Nelson : Yeah,…
